If I'm understanding how this works, you can use a scripting tool to do things like this. It's a powerful program for creating scripts to automate tasks like inputting text, hitting keystrokes in sequence with time delays, running programs, etc., that can be bound to any key or key combination.

It runs independently of the game on your PC in the background, so there should be no EULA issues... it just automates what you would normally do manually. I use it in hyper-realistic games with community patches to automate tedious complex tasks like getting ready for take-off. I don't use it in other games but would if manual engine management was worth the trouble to me.

Anyway, you should, for example, be able to make a script that runs from a key bind not used by the game, reads data from a local server, copies it into your clipboard, types T, inputs your message, CTRL-V to paste in the data, and hits ENTER to execute these key commands for you. If reading the local server data isn't possible, you could simplify it by just assigning something easy that can be done with one hand to output text such as SHIFT-1 = "I need help! (1,000m alt)", SHIFT-2 = "I need help! (2,000m alt)", and so on.

Hope this helps!

My guess is that their "rules" are just casting a wide net to minimize exploits that they cannot foresee, and they'll always label it as cheating for things they don't understand. As far as I know, there's no way for the game to detect if you're using an external scripting program since it's not altering the game files. I would also venture to guess that scanning your computer for things outside their game without your knowledge and permission would expose them to various legal issues.

Maybe someone specifically looking for it might detect a pattern in your chat, but that's highly unlikely. Additionally, automating tasks like manual engine control would be undetectable on the surface unless, once again, you provided them with a match playback file and they were actively searching for it or you outright informed them you were doing it. Promoting it would be the biggest giveaway, so technically the only mistake made was posting it in their forums where it could be easily seen.

Ultimately, they can't 'legally' dictate what you can use on your computer outside of their game, although it is their game, so they can ban users for an unlimited number of trivial reasons under their end-user license agreement. That's why it's worded the way it is; it's just lazy exploit enforcement. Anyway, I would say it would be perfectly safe to use scripting programs, just don't be obvious about it.

Personally, I don't use scripting in this game because there isn't much benefit to it, so I'm not really stressing over this. The game is pretty streamlined, so it's not like other games where you have to manipulate a dozen controls just to take off. I will even admit that their in-game communication system is quite effective in allowing players who speak multiple languages to communicate with each other. In the case of the script, do people really need you to tell them your altitude? You can basically see if teammates are above or below you from across the map. Given the company's strict approach to enforcement, any potential benefits just aren't worth the risk in my opinion.

In the end, you can submit game feature requests for things like this, and who knows... maybe they'll be implemented if the idea gains enough popularity. I know I would personally like to see the communication messages expanded, so perhaps that could be a better approach. It would also be less work if it's integrated into the game rather than dealing with scripting programs.

I do see where you're going with this. It would be easy, for instance, to create a script that enables manual engine control, closes your radiators, adjusts your propeller pitch, maximizes your throttle, etc., so all you have to do is push a button to achieve maximum escape speed. I suppose you could even create a script that, with some experimentation, makes your aircraft perform a complex maneuver at its maximum abilities when someone is tailing you.

I personally don't see an issue with this, though, as it's too much work for too little benefit over simply doing it yourself, and you'd be constantly trying to hit a moving target with the way the game developers change flight models more often than trends change. It also still requires that you know how to fly. Whether you do it or a script does it... what's the difference? You still have to know what to do.

My issue with this is that the game developers don't have the right to tell you what you can use on your PC while playing their game. What's next, you can't keep aircraft stats open in a document editor? You can't listen to music outside their channels? You can't watch videos of cats while climbing because you're bored? All these things are third-party programs that alter the individual's game experience and are technically against their end-user license agreement. Sorry, but I disagree with that.

I can see how it would be useful and definitely the least minor offense against their "no automation" rules. In the same light, it's only a (admittedly annoying) minor inconvenience to just create some shorthand lingo to relay alternative strategies in chat. I also see the point about it being easier for them to ban it all rather than deal with some subjective sliding scale on what can be scripted... hence opening this whole can of worms... and maybe some community members being a bit too sensitive over it. ;)

I do have to go back to my original opinion though that the game developers don't have the right to say what programs you can use on your PC (and probably can't detect them anyway) while playing their game as long as it doesn't alter the game itself. They might not like it but tough luck. Scripts won't give you that much of an advantage in this game anyway (or an advantage that others couldn't use) as flying is way too complex and dynamic. It's just not two-dimensional with a fixed number of possible movements like other games.

All scripting can really do is reduce tedious tasks and improve efficiency a little bit. Outside of that, you have to know how to fly and tell the aircraft what to do.

Just my two cents, but if bomber pilots wouldn't fly straight into a higher altitude enemy like lemmings, they might achieve different results.

I've certainly been guilty of flying bombers on constant suicide runs where I'd rush in, hit my targets, die, and repeat. Then I learned that the very definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over while expecting a different result... so I started thinking about trying different tactics and how to survive longer to inflict more damage. I often fly for one side, so I'll use the opposing side for some examples...

For instance, flying from a specific location as the opposing side, you can hit your targets and get out of there before enemy fighters arrive, loiter back over ship cover until the ground forces take control and the enemy numbers have been reduced by our fighters, allowing you to re-arm for another attack. Or skirt the right side of the map to take out the enemy tank column while the main battle is happening at the start.

For the opposing side in another region, try heading west along the map edge and then turning in to attack the carriers after passing the enemy airfield on your left. Take the time to bomb the carriers properly parallel to the deck rather than perpendicular to the ship where it's harder to hit them. You'll usually have time and face little to no opposition to do this. Then get out of there and return the way you came. You might even catch an enemy at the airfield on the way back. The opposing side knows that their enemies always climb to the south or go straight in low for the landing craft, and they have altitude and performance advantages, so why keep flying right into them? If three bombers just go west and do their job right, it can be game over for the other side.

Sometimes all you need to do is loiter and climb a bit at your spawn and let the fighters clear the skies before heading in... particularly on certain maps when flying as the opposing side. Let your teammates know this is your plan, and they'll appreciate having a mission with a purpose. It helps them to get their game face on. This is more effective than asking for escorts, in my opinion, as it's hard to protect bombers; it keeps fighters from getting the kills they want, and the fighters not escorting can get overwhelmed by the enemy's numbers because escort fighters are leaving their teammates short-handed.

It's also surprising how many multi-role fighter/bomber pilots never carry bombs on maps where they can make a significant difference. As one side on a specific map, a fully loaded aircraft can single-handedly slow or stop the ground war by bombing/strafing the vehicle columns on one side while also flying in a fighter role to take out enemy bombers that are usually operating in the same area. While its guns can't take out the tanks, I've noticed that taking out the anti-aircraft units and trucks makes our ground assets less distracted by them, allowing them to focus more on destroying the tanks for better effect. And hey, it's kills and points for you. It doesn't take long to help with the ground war, and you can then make yourself useful by attacking enemy fighters.

Anyway, I'm just saying use predictability to your advantage, keep adding different strategies to your repertoire, and it can increase your kill and win rates. It's more interesting and less frustrating than hitting a few targets and then giving the enemy a kill anyway.

All aircraft require mastering a certain skill set, but this doesn't diminish the characteristics I've highlighted. It has one notable strength, which is its climb rate, but it can still fall short in that area as well...

- Premium aircraft often get matched against opponents that are nearly equivalent in terms of your one strength while outclassing you in other aspects.

- It usually starts from the ground (or a lower altitude) against several aircraft that also possess excellent climb rates and higher starting altitudes. This undermines your climb advantage, forcing you to side-climb like many fighters, and your climb rate is not as beneficial above 6,000 meters against several enemy aircraft.

- You encounter situations where its comparatively lower top critical speed makes it challenging to escape after a dive attack or to stay out of gun range while climbing back up to engage in vertical combat against several aircraft that can still pursue you closely and maintain their position even in a lower energy state, allowing them to take shots due to their superior thrust, better energy retention, and good control at stall speeds. While this aircraft can help you gain altitude advantage, it lacks the other necessary attributes for a successful boom-and-zoom strategy, such as high critical dive speed, good maneuverability in a dive, sufficient armament for a potential quick kill, high top-level extension speed, and good energy retention.

- The controls of this aircraft become stiffer at higher speeds, making it difficult to keep your guns on a more agile opponent during a dive attack. It's also harder to shake them off your tail if they attack from behind. I'm not suggesting that you should let an enemy get right on your tail; many aircraft are fast enough to close in from 2 kilometers away, even if you have a slight altitude or energy advantage. However, you may lack the speed to escape, the maneuverability to turn back on them, and your climb rate may not be sufficient to out-climb them into a favorable attack position. Unless a teammate intervenes, you are stuck in the engagement and must prepare for them to catch you, which is not an ideal situation for this aircraft.

- This aircraft is one of the least durable in the game, so a single hit from some machine guns can significantly impair its maneuverability. It also has relatively weaker armament, meaning you can fire at opponents repeatedly in a close engagement with little effect, while they can land one hit on you and put you in serious trouble. This alone makes it a poor energy fighter, as it's common to exchange fire in close combat and become an easy target for other fighters that join the fray.

In any case, it's not a terrible aircraft and can be enjoyable to fly. I just don't believe it was worth the in-game currency I spent on it when there are many other standard fighters that are more competitive.

It doesn't have the worst stock syndrome in the game... but yes... you'll need it spaded to consistently out-power some of the tougher planes it meets like the British fighters, American fighters, and Soviet fighters. It should only take a night or two of hard flying to spade it at that tier. Once spaded, its advantages might seem slight but you'll be rewarded greatly if you use good discipline by climbing and boom-and-zooming. It's a wonderfully balanced plane where getting into trouble is usually pilot error.... most often from failing to observe one of these factors...

-You can typically gain the altitude advantage with a brief side-climb before turning in toward the enemy (I usually head toward our bases which attract bombers) and always seek to stay higher and faster than your enemies. You also want the right altitude advantage. 1km above them is a bit risky against some planes as they can still fly up your nose... even when you think they don't have the energy to do it. Around 1.5km-2km is ideal. Any higher means you'll gain too much speed in a dive attack (even if you fully cut the throttle) so you'll have to work your way down closer to your target before attacking.

-Always go for the highest enemy first. Be methodical in choosing your targets. Your altitude advantage affords you a good vantage point to decide on where to attack next. Be patient but not overly-cautious where you lack aggression. It takes more time to set up boom-and-zoom attacks than turn-and-burn fighting so maneuver and set up your attacks with purpose. Flying against turn-fighters is like playing checkers while boom-and-zooming is like chess. Being aggressive doesn't mean attacking all the time. It can mean pushing and baiting them all down into a disadvantage. It can mean disrupting attacks against your teammates. Don't target fixate on one enemy... you're fighting against the entire enemy team even if you can't see them all. Just remember that you're in a cage match where the team that kills the most fighters the quickest usually wins and this plane can be extremely disruptive.

-Commit and dive attack with confidence. If they quickly climb up to meet you, climb again hard, keep at least 1km distance, wait until they stall, use your flaps to turn back down on them quickly and it will be the easiest kill you'll ever get. I get many of my kills from energy trapping enemies and once you get good at it... you can bait them into this maneuver.

-Dive steeply as possible as it costs you no speed or energy to roll in the dive and allows you to keep lead on turners trying to squirm away. You can dive attack at shallower angles but you risk equalizing your energy with theirs if they're running fast which is bad. Many pilots will try to use this as a tactic so just keep some altitude in an extended chase.

-Ride your throttle to dive at the right speed. This is ideally fast as possible and it will take some practice on how to fly it on the bleeding edge of critical speed. You'll need that speed for the extend if you don't kill them. This plane is very well balanced and forgiving so you'll get the hang of it quick.

-Shoot machine guns far and cannons close. Conserve cannon rounds for sure shots. Shoot both when you have a close textbook attack setup. Cannon ammo is brutal but you have limited ammo. You have plenty of machine gun ammo but the machine guns can be hard to get a kill with... although you'll rarely run out so you're not totally defenseless. The higher the deflection angle... the more devastating your hits will be. Don't waste cannon ammo on bombers early in the game. (Feel free to take potshots with machine guns though.) Get the fighters first then cherry pick any surviving bombers/attackers.

-Don't dive below the enemy's altitude after you shoot as that's freely giving them energy you'll have to work to get back.

-Your biggest advantage is the ability to hit-and-run with impunity when done correctly so plan your escape/extend as part of your dive attack. Against a single enemy, extend in a direction that is behind their wing-plane so they have to bleed speed to come back around on you to pursue. Against a group of enemies, don't extend into the middle of them. Extend toward friendly planes, lines, and anti-aircraft fire... whatever advantages you can get as this is often when you're the most vulnerable. Know when to extend at a shallow climb angle or a steep one. Use shallow when you see the odds stacking up against you to put some distance between yourself and the enemy... then climb steeper to regain your altitude advantage at a safe distance to reset your attack. Use a steeper climb if you have a clear 1v1 energy advantage and want to press an attack.

-Be a good team player. Don't give up your altitude early in the match and dive with others on only 1 or 2 enemies like a lemming. Don't go out of your way to attack simultaneously with a teammate who is in control of an engagement unless you're already engaged. Stick around to help them in case they get overwhelmed though. Take turns boom-and-zooming. Climb when they dive and vice versa. Protect their six when they get tunnel vision in their attack or are being chased and hopefully they'll do the same for you. Work together to keep the enemy on the defensive and strip them of all their energy and advantages until one of you kills them. You might not get as many kills by being respectful and helpful but you'll likely suffer fewer deaths by keeping your friends alive which is the other half of your kill-to-death ratio. It's also a good way to be frugal with your altitude and ammo. Always kill the enemy if you have a shot and they're still a threat though.

-Avoid prolonged energy fighting. This puts you in danger of getting too low and slow

Very generally speaking, for the extend angle, a shallow approach is defensive and a steep one is offensive. Ultimately, it comes down to a bit of physics with potential versus kinetic energy, and this aircraft is better than what it faces in terms of gaining and converting one into the other. So if you have an altitude advantage, you can convert that potential energy into superior speed for your dive, attack, and maintain much of that speed in a shallow extend (around -10 to +10 degrees) to escape without getting shot, then convert it back into superior altitude when you're at a safe distance of about 1.5 kilometers away to attack again. It sounds like a lot, but when done well, you should be able to get yourself right back where you started, ready to attack in less than a minute.

A steeper climb right after a dive attack is much more aggressive and enters the realm of energy fighting. It also drains your speed faster, so you could be fully committing yourself in a fight to the death as opposed to hit-and-run tactics. Now instead of losing all your altitude, speed, and energy further with a turn-fight in the horizontal, you should energy fight them in the vertical. It can be as simple as quick successive boom-and-zoom attacks... dive-attack-climb-dive-attack-climb. It can involve using high loops, yo-yos, wing-overs, etc., to find a way to get over and behind the enemy. You just keep hammering down on them until they run out of altitude, speed, energy, and options. But I generally avoid doing this unless I have a clear advantage with the aircraft. It takes some experience to get a feel for when you can get away with doing it. It can energy fight well, but once again, you make yourself vulnerable by getting too low and slow while you have more control of the engagements with disciplined dive-hit-run-climb boom-and-zoom tactics, in my humble opinion. Ok folks. I cracked this nut for you. Explaining how to use manual engine control prop pitch with a specific aircraft to make them bleed speed for quicker and more controlled landings was getting me down-voted because you just want to go faster without damaging your engine. Fine. So here's the deal using the same knowledge...

I test flew a specific model and looked at the engine settings to see what auto engine management was doing and why it seemed so easy to damage its engine when trying to go faster using manual engine control prop pitch. The test was done using a reference model with 30 minutes of fuel, flying level at 1km altitude and at top emergency power speeds.

To match these conditions, I held efficiency at around 80% and limited RPMs to 2,600 which the simulation seems to prefer to prevent over-rev that damages the engine. So as the plane increases speed you need to continue reducing the prop pitch. However, the pitch percentage for fast speeds is much lower than what people thought. First off, it defaults at 50% when enabled which is a full 10%-20% higher than what you want when your throttle is maxed flying 400kph-500kph. No wonder why players were damaging their engines! Remember that speed, pitch and throttle are all connected so when going fast you need to quickly reduce the throttle, enable manual engine control prop pitch, adjust the pitch lower and then bring the throttle up smoothly so you don't damage your engine. It seems like a lot but should be quick and easy with practice. Anyway, I still had more RPM overhead in the last picture so some tweaking to the numbers should easily get it to 500kph which few aircraft the reference model is matched against can outpace at equal altitude/energy.

*An additional test revealed that the engine fails at 3,000 RPM so there's way more wiggle room than I thought. The belief that certain fighters from one country have to side climb because they're slower climbers than their opponents is actually untrue for many popular models from that country when it comes to overall climb to high altitudes.

This is because these fighters typically perform better than their opponents at higher altitudes. For instance, a specific model can climb from 0km to 7km altitude as quickly as a competitor in the same battle rating range, since the competitor might climb better up to around 4km, but the first model performs better above that. So it all evens out at the top. This is especially true since an artificial ceiling where performance is greatly reduced for all planes above around 6-8km altitude was introduced into the game a few months ago, which may have gone unnoticed by some players due to the drop in high-altitude performance.

Additionally, it's worth mentioning that the side-climb strategy tended to fragment teams from this country, while opposing teams would simply fly together as they climbed straight for the center to gain advantages in altitude and numbers. It also discouraged many pilots from this country from climbing at all, since it often resulted in few or no kills, while farming ground targets provided guaranteed rewards for progression.

Ultimately, the real issue has been that fighters from this country typically start on the ground, while many opposing fighters get air starts, and the side-climb is simply needed to make up the difference in starting altitude, not entirely due to climb rates. The reason I bring all this up is that an upcoming update will supposedly attempt to balance out these air starts, allowing fighters from this country to finally compete in high-altitude engagements and really shine, as they will be battling at high altitudes on more even terms where they were designed to excel.

I use a specific prop drag management technique for this reason. You see, in automotive engine management, prop pitch is linked directly to the throttle... so full 100% throttle gives you full fine prop pitch for maximum thrust (and prop drag but that doesn't concern us in this situation) with most aircraft. Conversely, zero throttle fully feathers your prop to coarse pitch... so cutting the throttle in a dive also reduces prop drag where you don't slow much at all in a dive. However, in this management technique, the prop pitch will stay where you set it independently of the throttle position... so when you cut the throttle, you still have maximum prop pitch for maximum prop drag but no engine thrust which helps to control your dive speed. Consequently, you can dive longer from higher altitudes where it's safer, prevent overshooting to stay locked on an opponent's tail, and it generally helps to stay out of wing rip and control freeze speeds (depending on the aircraft) with some simple throttle adjustments.

This means you need to be greedy about giving up too much altitude with the dive and need to extend in the horizontal after your attack to increase the gap with your opponent before converting that speed back into altitude again in a climb to reset the attack with an altitude/speed advantage. This is because fighters from this country generally have excellent speed retention when flying level-ish but poor climb rates where your opponent can catch you if you go too vertical too quickly as you'll bleed your speed advantage quicker than them in the vertical.

Anyway, it's a deceptively nuanced style of attacking that takes longer to cycle so it's ideal to have a teammate where you take turns hammering on an opponent as you go through the routine to keep your altitude and speed advantages while stealing your opponent's energy and options.
It's worth noting that until the 29th, 10 wins in the aircraft gets you the "244th Squadron Tail Marking" limited time decal which is pretty cool looking.
